background.definition: Ear and nose foreign bodies include animate and inanimate objects that are lodged in the external auditory canal or the nare.

list.listitem: Nasal FB is most common in children aged 2 to 4 years, whereas ear FB is most common among children aged 2 to 8 years.
Sex distribution for FBs of the ear is fairly even, whereas nasal FBs have a female predominance (female to male ratio of 1.9:1.0) thought to be due to hair beads.
The most common ear and nose FBs in children are food, paper wads, toy parts, hair beads, earring parts, and eraser tips.
Retained button batteries to the nose and ear are less common, but present a time-sensitive emergency, as liquefactive necrosis of surrounding tissues may occur within two hours.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Children with ADHD are more likely than the general population to present with ear or nose FB.

Because psychological problems are more common in children who present with FBs, consider assessment for psychologic disorders such as ADHD or autism or referral to a pediatric behavioral health specialist if clinically indicated.

list.listitem: Perform otoscopy or rhinoscopy to confirm the diagnosis of ear or nasal FB in a child presenting with unilateral mucopurulent discharge of the ear or nose. C
Consider radiography if a battery FB is suspected and rhinoscopy or otoscopy cannot adequately visualize it. C
Consider restraining an uncooperative child using a papoose board or performing sedation to safely visualize and remove ear or nasal FB. C
Providers should have a high index of suspicion for FB in children with risk factors and symptoms of retained FB.
Symptoms of ear or nasal FB include irritability and unilateral mucopurulent discharge of the ear or nose.
For nasal FB particularly, the most consistent findings are unilateral mucopurulent discharge and unilateral vestibulitis.

Physical examination of the nose involves performing anterior rhinoscopy to view the inner nare. If there is mucosal edema obstructing the view, a vasoconstrictor may be used to improve FB visualization.
Children presenting with ear FB may have otalgia, otorrhea, mild hearing loss, irritability, crying, or may be asymptomatic.
Physical examination of the ear involves performing otoscopy to view the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane.
Otoscopy may reveal signs of external auditory canal inflammation like edema, erythema, and otorrhea.
Laboratory examination is generally not necessary unless systemic infection is suspected.
If there is suspicion from the history that the FB is a battery, but it cannot be confirmed on exam, consider radiography to aid in identifying and locating the object.
Children who are young or are unable to cooperate with the exam may need to be restrained with a papoose board or sedated.
Proper instrumentation is key to the removal of FBs.
Remove a nasal FB using positive pressure, suction, or instrumentation, and choose the removal method based on available equipment and type of FB. C
Perform the “mother’s kiss” technique as the initial removal method for nasal FBs as long as absence of FB in the contralateral nare can be ascertained. C
Remove external auditory canal FBs using irrigation, suction, or instrumentation, and choose the removal method based on available equipment and type of FB. C
Do not use an irrigation method if the FB is known to be organic material since irrigation may cause the FB to swell and worsen canal obstruction. C
If the FB is an insect, kill or immobilize it first before attempting removal. C
Nasal FBs can be removed by positive pressure, suction, or instrumentation. The type of procedure depends on the equipment available and whether the FB is graspable or not.

The “mother’s kiss” technique is a useful and safe first-line option for a solitary unilateral nasal FB removal. This technique involves closing the unaffected nostril while the parent forms a tight seal with their mouth around the child’s mouth and uses forced exhalation to expel the FB out of the affected nare. This technique successfully removed 60% of nasal FBs in a systematic review of eight studies involving 152 children aged 1 to 8 years (95% CI 52% – 67%). No adverse events were reported in any of the studies, and the rate of use of general anesthesia was reduced from 32% to 2% in one study.

Alternatively, a bag-valve mask can be used in the same manner by forming a tight seal around the child’s mouth. A pop-off pressure relief valve should be employed with this method to prevent barotrauma.

A third positive pressure method that can be used is the nasal positive pressure technique. Oxygen tubing connected to an oxygen source and set at 10 L/min to 15 L/min is connected to a male-to-male tubing adapter, which is placed in the contralateral (unaffected) nostril. Generating positive pressure causes expulsion of the FB out of the affected nare.
These positive pressure techniques should not be used if a FB in the contralateral nare cannot be ruled out.
If the FB is graspable, such as something soft or irregularly shaped, like a piece of paper, cotton, foam, or a toy part, use alligator or Tobey forceps for removal.

If the FB is spherical or cylindrical, such as a bead or nut, use a curved or right-angle hook for removal by advancing the hook past the object, turning it 90 degrees, and then slowly withdrawing the hook and object together. Use of nasal forceps or hook successfully removed 100% of FBs in a retrospective study of 68 children with nasal FBs aged 1 to 12 years.

Alternatively, a round FB can be removed by the suction technique if a narrow enough suction tip is readily available. One example is the Schuknecht suction catheter, which has a narrow metal tip. This method of removal is best for smooth, round objects in the anterior nare.
Ear FBs can be removed by irrigation, suction, or instrumentation. The choice of procedure again depends on equipment availability and type of FB.

A meta-analysis comparing the success rate of ear foreign body removal attempts by EDs, primary care offices, and ENT clinics found that when the first attempt at removal is performed by an ENT specialist, there is a statistically significant increased rate of successful removal and the patient is less likely to require general anesthesia or sedation.

Irrigation can be used to remove small inorganic objects from the external auditory canal. Irrigation should be carried out using warm water and the spray should be directed behind the FB to aid in flushing it out of the canal.

Contraindications to irrigation include: A ruptured or perforated tympanic membrane Presence of a tympanostomy tube If the FB is vegetable material or a bean, as this will absorb the water and swell, causing further canal obstruction If the FB is a battery, as the irrigation can increase the potential for leakage, leading to liquefactive necrosis as well as alkaline burns
Similar to FB removal from the nose, if the object is graspable, alligator forceps can be used to remove it under direct visualization.

If the FB is not graspable, a narrow suction catheter such as the Schuknecht catheter can be used under direct visualization to remove the object. Alternatively, a right-angle hook can be advanced beyond the object, turned 90 degrees, and carefully withdrawn. These methods work best for FBs that are smooth and round and in the lateral one third of the external ear canal.

If the FB is a live insect, it should be killed prior to removal to prevent injury to the canal and tympanic membrane by the insect itself. This can be accomplished by putting mineral oil or lidocaine into the canal. The insect can then be removed by irrigation or by forceps.

In a retrospective review of 1197 children presenting with ear FB, 759 had initial removal attempts in the emergency department (ED) while 438 presented to the otolaryngology clinic. Of the 759 children presenting to the ED, an initial removal attempt was successful in 515 children. In the ED, irrigation was used in 201 cases, forceps in 289, and suction in 51; all three methods had similar odds ratios for successful removal.
Urgent referral should be considered if the FB is known to be a button battery or a magnet.
Referral to otolaryngology for nasal FBs should be considered if the first attempt has been unsuccessful.

Referral to otolaryngology for ear FBs should be considered if: The object is spherical The object is impacted in the external auditory canal or is up against the tympanic membrane The first attempt has been unsuccessful More than one instrument is needed for removal
Minor epistaxis is the most common complication of nasal FB removal and can usually be managed easily in the clinic or emergency department.

Attempts at removal of a nasal FB can result in the FB being pushed farther back into the oropharynx and thus risking aspiration; these cases should be referred to an otolaryngologist for further attempts at removal.
Button batteries can cause liquefactive necrosis leading to nasal septal perforation; therefore, these objects need to be removed as soon as possible after identification.

Removal of FBs from the external auditory canal can result in abrasions and bleeding of the canal, as well as more serious complications like tympanic membrane rupture and damage to the ossicles leading to hearing loss.

The possibility of additional unrecognized FBs as well as possible infection, such as acute otitis media, otitis externa, or sinus infection, should be ruled out by careful examination of both ears and both nares.

Successful removal depends on the length of time the FB has been in the nare or external auditory canal, the experience of the provider performing the procedure, instrument availability, and patient cooperation. C

Closely follow patients whose FB has been present for a long time and in whom multiple removal attempts were performed, given the higher likelihood of infection and significant inflammation in these patients. C
Remember to reinforce the importance of keeping small objects and toys with small parts out of the reach of young children. C
